7. Manufacture, life and complete economics

The production assumption is 100 cells per year, with 95% manufacturing yield, 7% factory overhead and development allocation across 500 cells. All complete-system prices are engineering estimates.

Capital boundary	Estimate
Repeat installed candidate	$1,146,941
Nonrecurring development program	$947,560
First program plus first installation	$2,092,606
Proposed smaller prototype build	$550,160
Separate prototype campaign	$11,049

The bill pays machining, heat treatment, prepared witness surfaces, weld inspection, assembly, rejects, sensors, bearings, drives, brakes, tool changers, depots, software preparation, calibration, anchors, transport, installation and retirement.

Important prepared-stock costs are:

Stock	Quantity	Cost
Bar bodies with prepared interfaces and gauges	85	$47,677
Factory crossframes	10	$29,735
Terminal cartridges	132	$114,256
Fixed host ports	126	$59,463
Stationary holder assemblies	6	$331,813
Separate strain probe	1	$16,332

Avoiding wafers does not establish a saving when the reusable construction requires this much supporting machinery and prepared stock.

Finite replacement assumptions

The costing model includes distinct renewal counters and calendar limits. Examples include:

Pin/bush fleet: introduced 1,000-operation or three-year interval.
Cup/adjuster mechanisms: introduced 5,000-operation interval.
Complete bar/terminal stock: eight years.
Factory frames/fixed ports: twelve years.
Gantry guides: 10,000 operating hours.
Holder brakes: conservative renewal before the most-used physical brake exceeds 500 stops.
Hydraulic seals/fluid: two years.
Gauge preparation/calibration: three years.
Batteries: four years.
PC/UPS: five years.

These are qualification requirements and cost assumptions. They are not measured lives. Commercial brake data provide finite torque, energy and stop limits, but do not establish the new installed assembly’s load, contamination and thermal performance.
